Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 25 July 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 039)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR FULLER: Good morning, Commissioner. First this
morning we have two witnesses being called concurrently
from the Royal Australasian College of Physicians,
Professor Inam Haq and Associate Professor Kudzai Kanhutu,
who are both online. I call those two witnesses.
<INAM HAQ, affirmed: [10.00am]
<KUDZAI KANHUTU, affirmed: [10.01am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FULLER:
MR FULLER: Professor Haq and Associate Professor Kanhutu,
my name is Dan Fuller, I'm one of the counsel assisting the
Commission and I'm going to be asking you some questions
this morning.
Firstly, each of you have signed off on a witness
statement dated 12 July 2024. Do you have each a copy of
that statement with you?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: That's exhibit H6.1 in the tender bundle.
Professor Haq, starting with you, have you had the
opportunity to review that statement recently?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: Is everything in it true and correct, to the
best of your knowledge and belief?
PROFESSOR HAQ: To the best of my knowledge and belief,
yes.
MR FULLER: Thank you.
Associate Professor Kanhutu, have you had the
opportunity to review the statement recently?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes, I have.

MR FULLER: Is everything in it true and correct, to the
best of your knowledge and belief?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes, it is.
MR FULLER: Thank you. Each of you have helpfully
identified in the statement which of you will speak to
particular topics, so I will try to address my questions to
the appropriate person, but please, if either of you have
anything to add on any of the questions that I've directed
to the other witness, please feel free to let me know.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Sure.
MR FULLER: Just starting with some background,
Professor Haq, can you describe your current role in the
college, please?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Sure. So I'm the executive general
manager of education, learning and assessment and my
portfolio is trainees and their training up and to
fellowship, from entry to basic training to exit as
fellows.
MR FULLER: For how long have you held that role?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Since January 2023.
MR FULLER: Have you previously held any leadership roles
within the college?
PROFESSOR HAQ: No.
MR FULLER: Associate Professor Kanhutu, can you please
describe your role?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes. I'm the dean of the College of
Physicians. My work portfolio encompasses workforce
planning, data research, and I also have leadership of the
research foundation that provides philanthropic grants to
our members.
MR FULLER: For how long have you held the role of dean?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: I commenced in September 2022.
MR FULLER: And did you hold any leadership role within

the college before that time?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Nothing that was paid. I did hold
some advisory roles and leadership roles as
a representative of the college on other bodies, but
non-college bodies.
MR FULLER: Do you also have a clinical role outside of
the college?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: I do. I still retain 0.3 clinical
work outside of the college of physicians but that's based
in Melbourne.
MR FULLER: Can you just tell us what that clinical role
is?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes, so I'm an infectious diseases
physician so I work in the hospital setting as well as
community-based care and refugee and migrant health.
MR FULLER: Thank you.
Professor Haq, do you have a clinical role as well?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes. I continue clinics at the Redfern
Aboriginal Medical Service in rheumatology, which is my
clinic.
MR FULLER: Thank you.
Associate Professor Kanhutu, starting with you, in
lines 68 and 69 of the statement, if you can just have
a look at those, you have described the college's remit as
being a "specialist education provider". Do you see that?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes. I do, yes, I see that.
MR FULLER: Do you see being a specialist education
provider as being the limit of the college's role?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: No, it's not, and I think what
I refer to, or what I refer to in terms of my understanding
of what the college remit is, is what is within our
constitution, which really clearly sets out our role as an
education provider as well as a steward of ethics for
physicianly practice within both Australian and

New Zealand. So my source of - my frame of reference
really is what's bound within the constitution, and which
is extensive, but really focused closely on education,
maintenance of professional standards for the specialties
that we have care of.
MR FULLER: Do you see part of the college's role as being
to advocate for the interests of its fellows?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: The advocacy that is stepped out in
the constitution mainly relates to advocacy for work that
relates to promoting good health and good health outcomes
for community and to the extent that revolves around
advocacy for certain groups of physicianly, I guess, craft
groups, yes, there is some overlap there for direct
advocacy for craft groups, for example, where we identify
that there are community care needs that aren't being met
due to either inadequacies in the way that our workforce is
being deployed to address those needs.
MR FULLER: Do you see it as being any part of the
college's role to advocate for individual fellows or groups
of fellows in relation to workplace disputes?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: No. We have traditionally not
engaged in any industrial matters. Our focus for advocacy
tends to be around topic areas or areas of community need,
where we can potentially provide support or can help
contribute to better outcomes for community. So the
advocacy lens is usually focused on community care needs
and gaps or perceived gaps there.
MR FULLER: Professor Haq, do you agree with that
description of the remit of the college?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, yes.
MR FULLER: Professor Haq, I understand - tell me if I'm
wrong - that you previously worked in the UK; is that
right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: That's right.
MR FULLER: Did you complete your training in the UK as
well?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I did.

MR FULLER: Are you familiar with the current way in which
accreditation, specialist accreditation works in the UK?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: Are we right in understanding that, at the
moment, at least, accreditation is not performed by
colleges but instead is performed by a central body?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I think it's by the GMC and their work,
yes, as I understand it.
MR FULLER: So not by individual colleges as it is in
Australia?
PROFESSOR HAQ: No, no, not in - not certainly the college
of physicians, anyway.
MR FULLER: Do you have a view as to the advantages or
disadvantages of that sort of model, where accreditation is
not performed by the colleges, compared with the model in
Australia?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, I think they're two very different
health systems and populations and I think the current
set-up is that the colleges have worked through
accreditation. I think there's always room for continuous
improvement there and working together. However, I feel
that, at the moment, the direction of travel that we're
going on with accreditation through the work of the AMC and
the National Health Practitioner Ombudsman has been really
helpful in bringing us all together to a common
understanding, working much more closely with the health
jurisdictions.
I think that the benefits of it being managed by the
colleges are that you have the subject matter experts as
fellows within the college, who understand the local
context, and are able to make informed decisions based on
that local context and understanding of the specialty field
as required.
I think it also is excellent as a peer review, as much
as anything else, and that, I think, engenders trust
between those being reviewed and those asking the questions
to allow, I think, a safe space for issues to be raised,

knowing that they will be dealt with in a manner that's
professional and appropriate.
So to answer your question, I think there is always
room for improvement but I think there are benefits of it
being managed at a college level. I think there - and
there are improvements in communication. If it was to be
a third party, let's say, who manages this, I think that
the process and procedures would have to be duplicated. It
may lead to a complexity in the system and communication
and decision-making, which, you know, health systems are
already very complex. Do we want to add complexity? And
it may take away some of that sort of positive constructive
approach of peer review and make it much more of a sort of
a top-down assessment.
MR FULLER: Associate Professor Kanhutu, did you have
anything that you wanted to say on that topic?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Look, I definitely concur with what
Professor Haq has articulated there. My experience of
accreditation has been there is so much to be gained from
the nuance and the understanding of context that we have.
So for Australia, being a very large country
geographically, a lot of the challenge that we find in
terms of accreditation really relates to local and
contextual factors and it's that benefit of having local
people and people who understand both the craft group and
the skill group from within the college who are there doing
the accreditation that I think makes it a really valuable
experience for both the accreditors themselves and also the
sites, and that understanding that it is truly a peer
review that's backed by a shared knowledge and a shared
appreciation of a framework that has been developed over
time.
So I think there is really benefit for having people
who are doing the accreditation having a close working
understanding of what it's like to work in various areas,
whether it's, you know, urban settings versus small or
outer metropolitan or even very small rural/regional remote
settings as well.
MR FULLER: When you refer to "craft group" and "skill
group" in that answer, can you just explain what you mean
by those groups, please?

A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes, so what I mean, both of them,
basically it's a synonym for the different specialties that
we have under our banner. We have, you know, 33
specialties and then we also have some legacy specialties
as well, and each of them can have very different needs and
very different ways of meeting their professional needs.
So for some of the specialties they're very clinically
oriented and are very much hospital based, and then we also
have specialties there, for example, public health, where
there is a really vast array of places and contexts where
those training needs can be met. I think that's the true
value of the way that we have accreditation running within
our colleges, that we're able to bring in subject matter
experts who are able to make that assessment on the ground
and understand is this setting fit for purpose and does it
actually meet the outcomes that have been set up for
a particular curriculum stream?
MR FULLER: In relation to those 33 specialties, they're
the ones we see in table 1 of the statement, which I think
starts at line 33; is that right?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: I will go back to that. Line 33?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, that's right, they're the training
programs, yes.
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes. Yes, correct.
MR FULLER: Thank you. Professor Haq, I think this is in
your section, so I'll ask you these questions. Are we
correct in understanding that a trainee with your college
will first undertake basic training in either adult
medicine or paediatrics and child health; is that right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, the majority will enter that way and
then enter into advanced training, but the chapters and
faculties may allow a trainee from other areas as well,
they're slightly more diverse in nature. But yes, the
adult and paediatric internal medicine route is usually
three years of basic training. You complete your
examinations and then you enter your chosen advanced
training stream.
MR FULLER: The chapters and faculties that you mention,
I think we see from line 11 of your, statement, they deal

with a subset of the 33 specialties; is that right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: No, they are separate. They are separate.
Yes, absolutely.
MR FULLER: In terms of the 33 specialties, after the
trainee, generally at least, has completed basic training,
then they undertake advanced training in one of those
specialties; is that right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, that's right.
MR FULLER: The only way to become a specialist in one of
the what I will call "physician specialties" is to complete
a training program through your college; that's right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, yes.
MR FULLER: As a consequence, you would agree that there
is no competition between your college and any other
training provider for specialist training in those fields;
that's fair?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I would say that we are the trusted
provider, as in the UK. You know, you alluded to the UK.
The college of physicians would be the provider of
physician training programs in the UK. We're similar,
yes..
MR FULLER: You would agree that because you are the
trusted provider, the only trusted provider of those
programs, it's important for your college to have fair,
effective and transparent processes for governance and
administering training programs?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Absolutely right.
MR FULLER: Professor, can you just explain to us what is
it that your college accredits? Is it sites or positions
or a combination? Can you just explain that, please?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes. So it is sites, and within that
there will be the number of positions that are within the
capacity to train of that site, dependent on the facilities
and the number of medical personnel there to supervise. So
it will be a mixture of the two. And that could be an
individual site or it could be a network of sites as well.

MR FULLER: Let me ask you first, why is it that the
college takes that approach to accreditation rather than,
for example, accrediting individual positions?
PROFESSOR HAQ: We don't cap, at the moment. I know some
colleges do, and we allow training sites to define what
they feel they need for training - in training based on
their infrastructure and resources. Then we would - you
know, then there would be a decision about whether that
number is correct based on the resources that have been
available and the guidance that the college gives. But we
do not cap positions at this stage.
MR FULLER: You mentioned the capacity to train guidance.
I might just show you that document so we're on the same
page. It's exhibit H1.36, [SCI.0011.0259.0001]. You'll
see it come up on the screen, Professor, in a moment.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Oh, yes.
MR FULLER: You don't need to worry about that.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: Do you see the document there on the screen?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I do.
MR FULLER: Is that the capacity to train guidance that
you were referring to?
PROFESSOR HAQ: It is, yes.
MR FULLER: Can we just scroll to page 2, please.
We see under the heading "How does the RACP assess
Capacity to Train".
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: In the first sentence, I think we see what you
have just told us that the RACP doesn't cap the number of
trainees; is that right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, yes.

MR FULLER: And then it goes on to say that the college
monitors numbers of trainees and where required modifies
the number when training provider accreditation standards
are not met. Can you just elaborate on what that means,
please?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I think that would be as part of the
ordinary accreditation cycle. If a place is accredited for
X trainees then the normal reaccreditation would be four
years or so and then that - the numbers would be reviewed.
If there was an issue with accreditation or conditions
applied to a site, then those numbers would be reviewed,
perhaps more on an interim basis, depending on the nature
of the conditions and the nature of any concerns that have
been raised.
MR FULLER: Just looking about halfway down this page, we
see a reference to the basic training accreditation
requirements and standard 5.2.1 --
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: -- which starts with a rotation supervisor.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes.
MR FULLER: Are we right in understanding that that is
effectively a ratio of the maximum number of trainees per
supervisor at a given site? Is that the right way of
understanding?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, that is guidance - that is guidance
on a ratio, yes.
MR FULLER: I see. So it's guidance. It's not the case
that if a site doesn't strictly meet that ratio, then it
will be denied accreditation?
PROFESSOR HAQ: No. No, I think at that point there would
be a decision based on in practice how does it work, and we
would triangulate data from the supervisors and the
trainees, and if there was an issue and actually it was
felt that more supervision was required that could then be
included in accreditation conditions or similar.
MR FULLER: Is there a similar requirement for advanced
training?

PROFESSOR HAQ: Those would vary according to - as you can
imagine, the very different number of specialties, and the
number of trainees is much smaller there per site, so
that's viewed - yes, there would be a view on that as well,
done through advanced training at a particular site.
MR FULLER: Who determines that view or position?
PROFESSOR HAQ: So it would be the advanced
training committee. There would be an accreditation visit.
There would be accreditation criteria for each specialty
that would be looked at and then the report would go to the
advanced training committee and there would be a decision
made there.
MR FULLER: Are there individual committees for each of
the 33 specialties?
PROFESSOR HAQ: So there would be - the advanced training
committee covers lots of or all aspects of training, but
also includes accreditation as well, as a decision-making
and review, yes.
MR FULLER: Associate Professor Kanhutu, was there
anything that you wanted to add on the matters I've just
been discussing with Professor Haq?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: No, nothing. Nothing extra.
MR FULLER: Thank you. We can take that document down,
thank you.
Professor Haq, you also mentioned the training
networks and, as we understand it, basic training, at least
basic physician training, is delivered within training
networks at least in New South Wales; is that right.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Mmm-hmm.
MR FULLER: Can you just explain how that works, please?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes. So that is - there would be like a
hub and spoke model, so there would be a sort of main
hospital that would be running the network and there would
be a mixture of metropolitan, regional and rural sites
assigned to that network and then trainees would move

around those sites during their training.
MR FULLER: Does the college have any role in developing
that network structure?
PROFESSOR HAQ: So that's where we work with HETI on that,
very closely, and I'm a member of their adult and - both
the adult council and the paediatric council, and we have
representation on the network group as well. So that's
where there's collaboration between the college and
external bodies.
MR FULLER: What do you see as being the advantages of
that structure for basic training in New South Wales?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Experience in different settings, yet
still under sort of a home network, so to speak, so they
understand where they sit. There is opportunity for more
than - you know, for communities of practice with the
trainees so they're not siloed on their own in particular
areas and I think it allows training to occur, as
I probably said, in different sort of areas, with different
areas of specialism, different population, so the trainees
can meet the curriculum requirements.
MR FULLER: I think we just missed the start of your
answer but I think you were referring to experience in
different settings.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, in different settings --
MR FULLER: Does that have to do with --
PROFESSOR HAQ: In different settings in sort of you know,
very specialist hospitals, with tertiary referrals maybe,
versus more regional and rural hospitals as well. So
a whole mix, yes.
MR FULLER: Is it the case that trainees are required to
rotate into, for example, rural and regional settings as
well as metropolitan settings? Is that right?
PROFESSOR HAQ: I think - with basic training I think
that's often a discussion for the network director of
physician education, to have with the trainee, as to where
they would be going on an annual basis to do their training
and if there are, you know, reasons why a trainee cannot go

to a particular place - and they may be family or personal
reasons - those would be taken into account. There's no
mandatory requirement for us at the moment to have
experience in one particular place but we see it as
desirable and part of our regional/rural (internet
interruption) - the longer a trainee - or a medical student
or trainee has experience in a non-specialist city centre,
the more likely they are to sort of stay there, and that's
part of managing workforce distribution, it is really
important.
MR FULLER: Is the college doing anything in particular to
help facilitate that?
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes. So across - so we are, through our
regional and remote strategy we will be working on - I
mean, New South Wales is probably, you know, sort of a bit
ahead of the game here. Through federal funding, FATES
funding, we are working on network models in other areas of
the country, particularly Western Australia in adults and
paediatrics, and Associate Professor Kanhutu is working on
those as well.
We actually very much want to facilitate working with
other health jurisdictions to ensure that trainees have
well-supervised experience rurally, because we now have
medical schools that are end-to-end rural training, we have
integrated training hubs for prevocational training, so
there's lots of opportunities now to ensure that we retain
that rural workforce in the appropriate places. And for
vocational training, networks, rural networks either purely
rural networks or networks that involve metropolitan and
urban settings as well is I think the way forward, and
New South Wales obviously is developed in that, well
developed in that regard. There are other areas that we're
working on to ensure that we can manage that as well.
Professor Kanhutu may want to speak to the FATES projects,
if you require.
MR FULLER: That would be helpful, Associate
Professor Kanhutu. Do you want to comment on that?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Sure. So we have two projects that
revolve around networked models. The first one is
a college-driven one, which is a project running in Western
Australia where they're looking to establish essentially
end-to-end training for adult medicine in rural, regional

and remote areas with a very brief period spent at a larger
site at the time that someone's performing their
examination. So the whole ambition there is to do as
Professor Haq alluded to, to allow people to spend as much
time as possible in a rural setting whereas traditionally
they would have had to rotate out or spend extensive
periods in metropolitan sites in order to meet their
training requirements.
So what we are enabling there is the ability to see
that we can actually allow people to develop all of their
core skills and competencies largely within a rural
setting, and then encourage them to stay there as well, and
that has been very well received for that Western
Australian cohort.
The other project we're working with is a consortium
project that involves a host of other colleges, including
college of surgeons and the medical administrators, which
is looking to establish what are the key components of
a successful network model, and then one of the outcomes
for the surgeons is to actually establish a rural network
in the Northern Territory.
If I can perhaps reflect on some of the comments
Professor Haq has made, one of the real benefits that we've
seen with the networked models is it's not only about
exposure to different context, it's the efficiencies that
it also allows and delivers for the sites individually.
One of the things that we've had as reflections from
the rural sites is the real challenge of recruiting, if you
are a stand-alone rural site. Often there is a sense of
prestige or allure for the larger metropolitan sites
because they often have access to research partnerships and
research linkages that can be a real drawcard, especially
for those specialties where there is an expectation that
there will be potentially an academic pathway or further
academic study as part of, you know, career progression.
There's also huge benefits at that basic training and
the advanced training level of having networks because then
people are able to share the same educational resources,
tutorials, and it really builds a sense of not feeling as
though, you know, they're a second-tier or third-tier site,
because people have an expectation that working within this
network, I will have access to exactly the - you know, as

many opportunities as I like, particularly if there are
some who are wanting to subspecialise. For example, some
of the cardiology specialties have subspecialties within
them, and it can be a bit of a challenge if people are
working in certain settings if they feel that they won't
actually have access or exposure to certain areas of
subspecialisation if they are locked into a single site.
So there are huge, I think, benefits to be gained from
those networked models, particularly as we're now working
to build them proactively and to design them, because many
of the existing networks, my observation has been, are
often legacy networks or networks that are built on
historical relationships and now what we're looking at, for
example, with the Western Australian example is to actually
say, "Look, if we're to start from scratch, how would we
build a network that is mutually reinforcing, that doesn't
have unnecessary duplication and also is networked in a
geographic way that potentially doesn't draw people that
still have to travel six hours or work in a network that's
actually unworkable for the individual and forcing them to
have to move house or move their families?"
That's really important that in this moment in time,
because we have so many of our trainees who are coming
through who are already postgraduate, have significant
commitments and often have had previous careers as well
that have bound them to particular geographies and giving
them that confidence that they can work in a network, still
have great exposure but aren't having to then recommit to
having to move extensively or disrupt that - I think that
sense of work/life balance that people increasingly value
and should really have access to, if we're serious about
wellbeing.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Yes, and I --
MR FULLER: Can I ask you - I'm sorry, Professor Haq.
PROFESSOR HAQ: Sorry, no, you finish your train of
thought with Professor Kanhutu.
MR FULLER: Thank you. Professor Kanhutu, can I just ask
you a few follow-up questions. Firstly, we've been talking
about FATES. That's a Commonwealth funding initiative
that's "flexible approach to training in expanded
settings"; is that right?

A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Yes, correct.
MR FULLER: Do you see any impediments to implementing
a similar model in New South Wales compared with Western
Australia?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: You mean a FATES funding model or --
MR FULLER: A similar networked structure to the one that
you've described in Western Australia that has been
implemented using the FATES funding?
A/PROFESSOR KANHUTU: Look, I think there's - I want to
say not "impediments", but barriers and enablers. I can
speak to the enablers and what we've seen is often the real
driver is having a committed group of clinicians who are
focused in understanding what is it that they're trying to
build and also have the support and buy-in of local
trainees who are saying, "Yes, that is exactly what we
need."
Where I think things can fall apart is when there
aren't those, I guess, relationship built bridges that
allow people to then wrap around that network and actually
formalise it and provide the governance structures. I feel
that that's the role that our college can play, is really
helping people to shape those connections and then make
sure that the accreditation model that is drawn up for that
network supports that to remain rigorous and balanced,
because a lot of this work, for better or worse, often
happen in its early phases through goodwill, and I think
what we'd like to see is that we support people to develop
networks where, firstly, there's a real recognition of the
amount of work that goes into building a robust and fit for
purpose network, because often the downfall is that, you
know, organically formed networks can suffer from having
individual or individual dependency as to, you know, there
is somebody who drove the beginning of the network, they
disappear or leave and then it falters.
I think what we would like to see is to give people
some of those guide ropes of how do you set up a network
for success, and that's one of the real outcomes that we
hope to achieve from that FATES project, the consortium
one, is: what does it take to do it right from start to
finish', what sort of resourcing is required; what sort of

background work do you need to do; and who do you need to
have over the lifetime of the development to make it
successful?
So I don't think there are any - you know, there will
be as part of this project, and one of them will be
a catalogue list or a summation of what are the barriers
and enablers for establishing a network. So absolutely
doable and there will always be those context dependent

there will be a process by which stakeholders will be
spoken to and engaged with to gather qualitative
information from a variety of places, such as - like,
definitely within NSW Health and what's going on on the
ground in our business; but also what we know that might be
happening in the university sector - for example, whether
a course is about to close or has closed, that's obviously
going to affect the supply calculations or projections.
Then the team will treat the data in a way that is
informed by the qualitative information that is provided by
the stakeholders with the expertise, that have real-world
understanding of what's going on with that particular
clinical workforce.
Q. So that's on the supply side?
A. No, that's on the demand side.
Q. The demand side?
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Can you just define for me what is
the supply side and what is the demand side?
A. So at a very high level, the supply is where are we
getting the work - where is the workforce coming from and
what is influencing where they're coming from? That's at
a very basic level, yes.
Q. And the demand?
A. And demand is what is creating the demand for that
workforce? So what's changing in the community or the way
we provide services or change in the population? So as
a very general example --
Q. It's the demand for healthcare services that you're
talking about?
A. Demand for healthcare services, yes, which will be

influenced by a variety of things.
Q. Like ageing, for example?
A. Like ageing, chronic disease, population growth,
immigration, socioeconomic determinants, and that will
differ from district to district. So whilst there will be
trends that will be looked at at a state level, things will
differ from district to district because populations are
different, demands are different. For example, from
a metropolitan to a rural.
Q. And how far in advance does the modelling look? Are
the models producing predictions for, "This is likely to be
the workforce required in two years' time"; "This is what
it's likely to be in 10 years' time"? How does it work?
A. So currently the modelling is being done to 2040, so
about 15 years ahead.
MR GLOVER: Q. What sort of data goes into the modelling
for projections out to 2040?
A. That's a question I can't confidently answer for you.
So either - we could gather that information, or Richard
Griffiths is appearing later in the hearing and he may be
better placed to give that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. The uncertainty in the inputs in
the model not so much the supply side, because you
currently know who is doing what courses and what the
numbers are; the greater analysis perhaps and the more
difficult inputs is what is going to be the demand?
A. Yes, that is the most complex part of it. So the
supply side, for an example, if we were looking at nursing
and midwifery, things like fertility and birth rates would
be important in considering that workforce, where that
might not be so important with other workforces, and so
it's a bit more - it's a bit easier to identify what's
coming in to that side of the model.
The demand side is definitely the most complex, and as

a global pandemic, such as the introduction of the NDIS,
and really understanding the full impact of that policy
over time, and so when --
Q. Also, I suppose, if there are different new models of
care?

A. Correct.
Q. They might compress periods of morbidity?
A. Yes.
Q. And if, worst case scenario, we might have longer

A. Yes.
Q. -- and that creates an uncertainty, I suppose, in

A. Correct.
MR GLOVER: Q. Can I take you to paragraph 2(b), please?

psychology.
Q. Can I take you to paragraph 2(c), the last of the

A. So that's probably the reason for the establishment of
the unit and noting that I've been in this role for about
11 months now, is - I'm just thinking of a succinct way to
answer this. So on commencement in the role, the health
system in response to the future health strategy and the
health professionals workforce plan identified, via chief
executives, top priorities that needed to be looked at
where there were innovative models of care that had been

identified as a priority, and my unit leads some of those

or is involved in most of those areas and those projects.
Q. In what way?
A. So my team has the central expertise around the health
professional workforces at the state level. We engage with
other stakeholders, including the Agency for Clinical
Innovation, Health Education and Training Institute,
Clinical Excellence Commission and other internal branches
within the ministry like the nursing and midwifery office,
and we have a very close, ongoing relationship with local
health districts which I described before in our
stakeholder engagement.
So the unit and my role is like a bit like a broker
but also knits or stitches together and creates traction
between those various groups that have particular focus,
but really, the workforce model and what the workforce is
doing is a critical element of operationalising any changes
to models of care or service delivery, and particularly
when you're looking at it from a state scaling perspective.
So we don't just look at numbers and what's where;
it's who are the people and what are they doing and what do
we need them to do and therefore, are there different ways
we can do that or are there areas of red tape or barriers
we have to unlock that will then allow districts to just
get on with it and implement the changes they need to?
Q. And under that umbrella, is one of the pieces of work
that your team has been involved in looking at what is
described as "scopes of practice"?
A. Yes.
Q. If we go ahead to paragraph 43 of your statement,
please. By way of introduction to this topic, you tell us
that there is no universal definition for scope of
practice, with professions applying it differently.
Appreciating that there might be many variations, what are
the general differences between the way it is utilised?
A. So just going back to the term "scope of practice",
that term and the way it's applied, as you have just said,
is bandied around differently in different conversations,
and often people think they're all talking about the same
thing and they're not.
So, for example, one profession might talk about
advanced scope; another profession might talk about top of

scope; another profession may talk about extended scope.
Often they think they're all talking about the same thing
or they're all talking about different things and sometimes
it's hard to tell.
For this Inquiry, we did prepare some briefings to try
and simplify the use of those terms, and that's one of the
things that our unit is doing in our engagement with
stakeholders, so we can have meaningful conversations.
Because it's like speaking five different languages, and
I feel like I've moved to Switzerland in this job at times,
to try and have a conversation with people that come from
very different frames of reference, and even at the
national level in my engagement with AHPRA, it's something
that's acknowledged that different boards and professions
will categorise things differently and apply it to how
their professions have evolved over time, yes.
Q. So that we make sure we are understanding each other,
when you use "top of scope", what do you mean?
A. So if we look at scope, which broadly would be things
like the training someone's done, the registration they
need to have, the legislation or licences they need to
operate with or within, and then the context of where they
work - so those are the kind of, just roughly, things that
would make up a scope of practice.
When we talk about "within scope", it means that that
professional person might have a broader range of things
that they could do, but in the context of this role or our
discussion, we're talking about things that are within
scope. If we're talking about "full scope", which is also
a term that's used a lot, that means the person can or is
operating across the entire spectrum of what they're able
to do in that context, and that might be, for example,
someone working in a rural area or in a generalist role
where they need to do all the bottom and top end of that
job because they don't have other people to do it or that's
just the way it's designed.
"Top of scope" is where everyone wants to be, which is
as a health professional, I have been trained to do lots of
things, but I really like to do what I'm really good at,
what I'm really expert at and what the patients really
need, and that's where you move up into the top of scope,
but this bit in the bottom may be where an assistant or
a piece of technology or a decision-making framework or

something else has been put into place to take that, let's
call it, lower-value work or work that doesn't require that
higher level expertise; or it could be that, in that
context, you have multiple professions working together,
there's an overlap in what is at that bottom, but by
recognising that and not duplicating that work, you're
allowing people to push their effort to the top of scope in
that model.
Then, finally, if we're looking at what's "out of
scope" or what we're trying to look at, whether it's
advancing or extending, but I'll use the term "out of
scope", that's where there's the opportunities to go: is
there some low-hanging fruit there because of some kind of
regulatory licensing, training, whatever issue it might be,
it's not currently in scope, but if we do something, we can
put it in there; like, it's not unachievable.
Q. And if a plan referred to "examining opportunities to
extend scope", would that be in that third category that
you have just described?
A. Yes, so I've probably - again, I've fallen into that
trap, used that word. "Extended scope" is probably a word
a probably need to stay away from. But really, it's about
at a foundational basis, top of scope, out of scope, and
then different professions will use those terms as it
applies to their individual practice. So as an OT, you
know, my normal scope is this, but as a profession, the
profession might be looking at how they could advance or
extend the scope of the profession. Does that make sense?
Q. Yes. In an earlier answer you said that everybody
wants to be at top of scope?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Why?
A. Anecdotally from engagement?
Q. Your understanding and experience?
A. From my understanding? That provides a higher level
of satisfaction for clinicians. They enjoy being well
utilised. They're highly trained people. Generally they
come into health care because they want to help people,
they want to do the best that they can and it allows them
to operate in a more autonomous way, where they feel like
they're using all their muscles and their capability on
a daily basis, and therefore feel more valued.

Q. Accepting that those principles are important from
a system perspective, are there other system advantages to
having clinicians operate at the top of scope?
A. Yes. So I think it's minimising duplication and
maximising your bang for buck. So if you're paying for
someone who has a higher level of capability than you're
using then you are not getting value for money in what
you're asking that person to do.
Q. In paragraph 44 of your statement you tell us that
there are a number of barriers, however, which impact on
the ability of clinicians to operate at their top of scope,
and you give some examples. If we just start with the
example in paragraph 44(a), "Workplace culture and
attitudes of individual clinicians and managers which can
prevent collaborative and transdisciplinary working", how
might the culture and those attitudes manifest to create
a barrier to clinicians operating at top of scope?
A. In many ways. So it could be as simple as people
working in a service or a team where there is an individual
or a group of individuals that is very comfortable with the
way things are working, they don't want to change the way
things are working and, therefore, might behave in a manner
that is recalcitrant or not collaborative in the efforts of
other clinicians and/or leaders, managers, executives, to
improve or change a service for the benefit of patients.
You can talk about things like, you know, let's assume
that the evidence says it's a good idea that scopes of
practice say it's fine that there's no legal impairment,
that we can unlock all the red tape, so let's say we can
fix all those things. If there's someone who's senior
enough, powerful enough and with a loud enough voice that
says, "This is unsafe", and they say it repeatedly enough,
then people will believe that. And that's one of the
things clinicians will often first say when they are
uncomfortable, "This is unsafe. This is unsafe." And that
happens a lot, or, "No, I don't think that person can do
that, I don't think that's in their scope of practice". So
where you've got other professions commenting on what
another profession is trained to do or capable of doing.
And that may be because that's that person's genuine belief
or that they're not informed or that they're scared because
they don't know what they don't know or there's a genuine
safety concern that we're not aware of that hasn't been
properly articulated or explained.

Q. How prevalent is culture and attitudes of the kind
that you've just described across the system, to your
observation?
A. So I would say there are pockets of outstanding
excellence, and where you get particularly a senior medical
clinician that is really on board, focused on the community
and really empowering and valuing the multidisciplinary
team they work with - and that is allied health, that is
nursing/midwifery - it can be amazing accelerator. It's
like magic, it just unlocks all of the barriers and they
just focus on the outcome and get it done, and there are
pockets of that all over the place.
However, I would say that it is definitely a massive
challenge and is quite prevalent across the state, and that
makes it difficult for particularly our next generation of
clinicians that are coming through, that are coming out of
university and are very excited and they're innovative and
they've got ideas and they're obviously tech savvy and they
want to do amazing things, and that can be a real challenge
to come up against when they suddenly enter a system like
NSW Health. So - yes, I'll stop there.

et cetera.
A. Mmm.
Q. You gave some examples in that last answer. Is there

A. Yes. I'm just trying to think of which one. Can
I just read the paragraph again?
Q. Of course you can. Take your time.
A. Could you just ask me the question again, sorry?
Q. Yes. So in the answer you just gave, you mentioned as

A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. What I was just inviting you to do, in relation to

A. So again I'll talk about - so real or perceived, so
from a cultural perspective - I will just give two
different examples, if that's okay.
Q. Of course.
A. So from a perceived perspective, I can talk about
a conversation I was perhaps having the other day around
governance. So if we're going to put in a new model and we
decide that we want to put in a different type of health
professional than we've put in before, we need to make sure
there's a good governance of that person to make sure that
they have good clinical support, they know who their
operational manager is and they know who their professional
line is.
So with health professions, best practice requires
that you have an operational manager so you know who you
report to; you might have a clinical line, which is who's
responsible for the overarching care of the patients in
that setting; and then a professional line, which is
someone from your own discipline. The way those three
lines behave is different across professional groups.
So, for example, in nursing/midwifery, they're
normally all the same person. In medical, there might be
a combination of that. In allied health, we're very used
to - and I say "we", because my background is occupational
therapy - used to working in a matrix structure. So if
we're putting someone into a model of care that is an
autonomous clinician that can work really well without
being, you know, high degrees of supervision, and another
professional group might find that very concerning because
the three lines of governance are not aligned to the one

therefore, they will raise concerns about, "Well, what

my unit, in looking at models we might be trialling at

Excellence Commission, the chief health officers unit, as
well as the local clinical governance groups in the

bee haven't considered in the design of the models, which
therefore we can confidently respond to any concerns people
might raise, whether they are real or perceived, about
safety.

medicine, nursing, midwifery, paramedicine, how that has

to then have a conversation to lift people up and say,

continues to be challenging and I recognise that that's
a key component of my role in the unit and with our

conversations, as uncomfortable as they are, yes.

conversations?

where we've started to have conversations in a variety of
forums for different reasons, generally, when you give
people the time to ask questions and be curious and you
listen to them - and I think that's the key, we've got to
listen to people and what their concerns are; however, then
have a robust conversation in an evidence-based manner
about genuine concerns versus just poor attitude, and then
to be able to distil, well, what is it that we need to
genuinely address and what is it that's another issue?

engaging in the dialogue.
Q. Can I take you back to 44, and this time to

A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Is there any other work being undertaken in relation
to the barrier that you identify in paragraph 44(b)?
A. Yes, I can give a couple of examples.
Q. Please do.
A. So one is, in my portfolio I'm responsible for the

health practitioners and growing the number of places that
they can work in multidisciplinary teams across the state.
So one of the pieces of work is where Aboriginal health
practitioners are trained and able to do things like
administer intramuscular injections, but because of the way
they're employed within NSW Health, they may not
necessarily be doing that all the time - sorry, let me just
take a step back. This is about Aboriginal health
practitioners and enabling them to vaccinate the Aboriginal
community.

not possible, so we've worked with the immunisation unit
and Western New South Wales, who had raised that they
wanted a group of their Aboriginal health practitioners to
start vaccinating the community this year with Fluvax -

between 5 and 65 the Aboriginal population has a very poor
vaccination rate compared to the rest of the population.

the immunisation unit, they put in place an authorising
instrument to enable Aboriginal health practitioners to
vaccinate with the flu vaccine and also have a state
standing order to administer adrenaline, so that in the
case of an anaphylactic reaction they could administer
that, and that would mean that they could do that
independently without having to get a direction repeatedly
from a medical officer. Again, if you don't need to have
that person in the team, if there's an instrument that
allows you to just get on with it with the appropriate
governance in place, that makes it --
Q. So just from that answer, do I understand that there
have been some reviews undertaken of a range of legislative
barriers to particular clinicians performing particular
services, with a view to removing them?
A. Correct.
Q. Can I take you ahead to paragraph 44(d), please.
There you tell us that in some cases, employment conditions
arising from industrial instruments may be a barrier?
A. Yes.
Q. What work is being done to overcome those barriers?
A. So NSW Health, as well as the industrial associations,
are commencing a process of award reform and members of my
team are involved in each of the various working parties
around medical awards, allied health awards and Aboriginal
health practitioner awards, and other awards that may
affect our health professional workforces. So that work is
occurring. Yes.
Q. So what type of barriers are created by the industrial
instruments to permitting clinicians to operate at the top
of their scope?

The second example is the health professionals award,
which currently encompasses 18 allied health professions,
treats things like on-call allowances differently between
professions, and then the other five professions are

employed under different awards again, so if you're trying
to look at designing a model of care where you're wanting
professions to behave in a similar way, it can make it
difficult, as a manager, to do that and it may then
influence your choices about whether or not you would
include certain professions in your service model.
Q. And that's why you tell us in your statement that
those instruments are operating as a barrier to the
implementation of the innovative model?
A. Correct.
Q. In paragraph 45 you refer to the scope of practice
review.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Then in paragraph 46 you tell us that your unit is
coordinating the statewide response, and that, in doing so,
it has been a significant opportunity for NSW Health to
contribute to the process of identifying and addressing
barriers experienced by primary health care professionals.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. What barriers have you identified to primary health
care professionals in operating to their optimum scope of
practice?
A. So as far as the review is at, and noting that the
outcomes have not been finalised, the barriers that have
been identified are very similar - so are things like
access to training and education; the existing regulatory
policy and legislative requirements. So they operate
under, obviously, federal policy, largely, but also
state-based policy will be influencing what they can and
can't do. The way that work is arranged and funding is
applied to particularly professions that are not general
practitioners, in being able to deliver care to the
community, and that's obviously out of our scope; and
technology and the availability and use of technology in
being able to deliver care, and particularly whether or not
that attracts funding.
So noting that some of those things are out of our
scope, however, the principles are also applicable to the
work that we do in NSW Health.
Q. In that answer you referred to professions other than
general practitioners. Who did you have in mind?

A. Physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech
pathologists, even nursing, midwifery. So people who would
be considered as members of the multidisciplinary team that
are required to deliver care to populations that have
chronic and complex issues, so where the general
practitioner might have a short - you know, may coordinate
care or identify issues that need to be addressed, the
ability of that patient to then be able to go and access
things like podiatry, speech pathology, dietetics can be
limited by the things that I have just outlined.
Q. In paragraph 47 - and you touched on this in an
earlier answer - you tell us that the general findings from
that review are expected to be transferrable to the
New South Wales public health system and will likely assist
in informing ongoing statewide reforms. Why do you hold
that view?
A. So looking at the early themes that have come out of
that review and through our work in coordinating the
responses for New South Wales health system, the items that
I just listed around training and education being a barrier
